lesson.title: One Return Statement, Several Answers
lesson.summary: A function can only return one object, but Python lets that object be a tuple, so a single return statement can hand back several values at once.
lesson.body:
When you learned about Return Values, the rule was simple: a function hits a return statement and hands one object back to whoever called it. But plenty of real computations naturally produce more than one useful result. Finding the smallest and largest number in a list, splitting a full name into a first and last name, converting a temperature and also reporting whether it is above freezing: each of these feels like it should return two answers, not one.

Python resolves this without breaking its own rule. Because a Tuple is just a single object that happens to hold several values in order, a function can return one tuple and it will look, and behave, like it returned several things at once. Write return a, b and Python packs a and b into a two-item tuple before handing it back. The function still obeys the one-return-value rule; it just chooses a value that is itself a small container.

def min_and_max(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)

result = min_and_max([4, 1, 7, 3])
print(result)
print(type(result))

low, high = min_and_max([4, 1, 7, 3])
print(low, high)

Running this prints (1, 7) on the first line, then <class 'tuple'> on the second, confirming that result really is a tuple and not two separate values floating around. The third print, after the call low, high = min_and_max(...), shows 1 7: the caller pulled the tuple apart into two named variables in the same line it called the function. That splitting apart is called unpacking, and you will study it in detail soon; for now, just notice that it is what makes multiple return values feel natural to use even though, underneath, only one object ever traveled back from the function.

The practical takeaway is that whenever you see a function called with two or more names on the left of an equals sign, like low, high = min_and_max(numbers), you are looking at a function that packed its results into a tuple and a caller that immediately unpacked them again.
